\chapter{Euler Hamilton}
%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Euler Hamilton}

% Generated by scripts/blueprint_from_docstring.py from TCSlib.GraphTheory.Core.EulerHamilton.
% Prose is extracted from Lean docstrings; verbatim book quotations are excluded.

\begin{definition}[$G$ is eulerian: it has a closed Euler trail (an Euler tour)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsEulerianGraph}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsEulerianGraph}
\leanok
\texttt{$\exists$ u, $\exists$ p : G.Walk u u, p.IsEulerian} --- a closed walk using every edge exactly
once.  Mathlib's \texttt{Walk.IsEulerian} is defined via \texttt{List.count} on \texttt{p.edges},
which is why \texttt{[DecidableEq V]} is genuinely required here and not merely
convenient.

Note the book's three-way vocabulary collapses in Lean: \texttt{IsEulerian} already
implies \texttt{IsTrail}, so "closed Euler trail" and "Euler tour" are the same
predicate on a \texttt{Walk u u}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Component count $\omega(G)$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.numComponents}
\label{SimpleGraph.numComponents}
\leanok
\texttt{Nat.card G.ConnectedComponent}, following Mathlib's own idiom in \texttt{Tutte.lean}.
Deliberately \textbf{not} named \texttt{omega}, which is a tactic.

Theorem 4.2 only, as the left-hand side of the toughness condition
$\omega(G - S) \le |S|$: a hamiltonian graph cannot fall into many pieces when few
vertices are deleted.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[join]
\lean{SimpleGraph.join}
\label{SimpleGraph.join}
\leanok
$G \lor H$, rebuilt on Mathlib: within-side edges from $\oplus g$, all cross
edges from \texttt{completeBipartiteGraph}. \texttt{symm}/\texttt{loopless} are inherited from $\sqcup$.

Lay the two graphs side by side keeping all their own edges, then add every
edge running between them.  The book's $G + H$ (disjoint union) is Mathlib's
$\oplus g$, and "joining each vertex of $G$ to each vertex of $H$" is exactly
\texttt{completeBipartiteGraph V W}, so

    join G H = (G $\oplus$g H) $\sqcup$ completeBipartiteGraph V W

on carrier $V \oplus W$.  Building it as a $\sqcup$ of two existing graphs means \texttt{symm}
and \texttt{loopless} are inherited and need no proof.

The building block of the graphs \texttt{Cmn} below.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$C_{m,n} = K_m \lor (K_m^c + K_{n-2m})$, with $+$ the Mathlib disjoint sum $\oplus g$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
\label{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.join}
Take $m$ "hub" vertices forming a complete graph, $m$ isolated vertices, and a
complete graph on the remaining $n - 2m$; then join every hub to everything
else.  Carrier \texttt{Fin m $\oplus$ (Fin m $\oplus$ Fin (n - 2 * m))}, with $K_m^{c} = \bot$ on \texttt{Fin m}.

Degrees: the $m$ hubs have degree $n - 1$, the $m$ isolated vertices have degree
$m$, and the remaining $n - 2m$ have degree $n - m - 1$.  That is the degree
sequence Theorem 4.6 majorises against.

\textbf{!} The side condition $1 \le m < n/2$ is \textbf{not} carried in the type.  For $m = 0$
or $2m > n$ the definition still elaborates (with $n - 2 * m$ truncating to $0$)
but no longer matches the book's figure.  Callers must supply the bound.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The sorted (ascending) degree sequence of $G$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
\label{SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
\leanok
Simply list how many neighbours each vertex has, smallest first.

Degree is written \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet v)} rather than \texttt{G.degree v}, so the
definition works for any graph on a \texttt{Fintype} without threading a
\texttt{DecidableRel G.Adj} instance; the two agree when $V$ is finite.

The book indexes from $1$ ($d_{1} \le \dots \le d_\nu$); the Lean list is $0$-indexed, so the
book's $d_m$ is \texttt{degreeSequence.getD (m - 1) 0}.  Statements below that quote
Theorem 4.5 must account for that shift.

Chv\'atal's Theorem 4.5 reads hamiltonicity off this list alone; Theorem 4.6 and
Corollary 4.6 compare two such lists via \texttt{DegreeMajorised}.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$G$ is degree-majorised by $H$: same order, and every sorted-degree entry of $G$ is $\le$ the\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised}
\label{SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised}
\leanok
\uses{SimpleGraph.degreeSequence}
Line up both degree sequences in increasing order and compare entry by entry;
$G$ is degree-majorised by $H$ when $H$ wins or ties at every position.

Quantifying over \emph{all} $i : \mathbb{N}$ with \texttt{getD i 0} rather than over \texttt{Fin $\nu$} is
deliberate: past the end of both lists the comparison is $0 \le 0$, so the extra
indices are harmless and no bounds proof has to be threaded through.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[One Bondy--Chv\'atal closure step: add a nonadjacent pair whose degree sum is $\ge$ $\nu$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
\label{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
\leanok
Look for two vertices not yet joined but which between them already have at
least $\nu$ neighbours; Lemma 4.4.1 says adding the edge changes nothing about
hamiltonicity, so add it.  Repeat until no such pair is left.

\texttt{ClosureStep G H} captures a \emph{single} such addition, \texttt{H = G $\sqcup$ edge u v}.  The
closure is then reached by \texttt{Relation.ReflTransGen ClosureStep}, and "no such pair
remains" is expressed at the use site as $H = \top$ or as the absence of a further
step, rather than by a fixpoint operator.

Defining $c(G)$ as a function presupposes Lemma 4.4.2 --- that the result is
independent of the order in which edges are added --- and that lemma is itself one
of the chapter's results.  Positing the fixpoint would therefore assume what the
chapter sets out to prove.  Using the step relation keeps the development honest;
the price is that statements below quantify over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep}
chains instead of mentioning $c(G)$ directly.

Degree is \texttt{Nat.card (G.neighborSet $\cdot$)} so the relation is well-typed for
arbitrary graphs on $V$ without a \texttt{DecidableRel} instance.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$G$ is Hamilton-connected: every ordered pair is joined by a Hamilton path (Ex 4.2.11)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
\leanok
Not merely that \emph{some} spanning path exists, but that both endpoints may be
prescribed arbitrarily: \texttt{$\forall$ u v, u $\ne$ v $\to$ $\exists$ p : G.Walk u v, p.IsHamiltonian}.

Substantially stronger than being hamiltonian, and correspondingly forces many
edges --- part (a) is \texttt{hamiltonConnected\_edge\_bound} below, part (b) is
\texttt{exists\_extremal\_hamiltonConnected}.

The book's $[x]$ here denotes the ceiling, so $[\tfrac{1}{2}(3\nu+1)]$ is $(3 * \nu + 1 + 1) / 2$
in natural-number division.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$G$ is hypohamiltonian: not Hamiltonian, but every vertex-deleted subgraph is (Ex 4.2.12)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.IsHypohamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.IsHypohamiltonian}
\leanok
The graph just barely fails to be hamiltonian: no spanning cycle itself, yet
deleting any single vertex repairs the defect.

$G - v$ is \texttt{G.induce (\{v\}$^{c}$ : Set V)}, whose carrier is a \emph{subtype}, so each
\texttt{IsHamiltonian} obligation is about a different vertex type.  The \texttt{open scoped
Classical in} above the definition is what discharges the resulting
\texttt{Fintype}/\texttt{DecidableEq} instances on those carriers.

\texttt{petersen\_isHypohamiltonian} below --- the exercise itself.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.1: a nonempty connected graph is eulerian iff it has no odd-degree vertex]
\lean{SimpleGraph.euler_tour_iff_no_odd_degree}
\label{SimpleGraph.euler_tour_iff_no_odd_degree}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsEulerianGraph}
Every visit to a vertex consumes one edge coming in and one going out, so the
edges at each vertex must pair up.

The ($\Leftarrow$) direction is a \emph{minimal counterexample} argument.  In Lean that is
strong induction on $\varepsilon(G)$ --- the book's "choose such a graph with as few edges
as possible" --- generalised over the graph, since $G'$ is a different graph on
(the subtype of) the same vertex type.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.1: a connected graph has an Euler trail iff at most two vertices have odd degree]
\lean{SimpleGraph.euler_trail_iff_le_two_odd}
\label{SimpleGraph.euler_trail_iff_le_two_odd}
By Corollary 1.1 the number of odd-degree vertices is always even, so "at most
two" means exactly $0$ or $2$.

This is the precise answer to the K\"onigsberg question and to exercise 4.1.1: a
figure can be drawn "without lifting the pen and without retracing" exactly when
it is connected and has at most two odd-degree vertices.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.2: if $G$ is hamiltonian then $\omega(G - S) \le |S|$ for every nonempty proper $S$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_toughness}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_toughness}
A hamiltonian graph is held together by a single cycle through every vertex, and
a cycle is hard to shatter: removing $k$ vertices from it leaves at most $k$
arcs.

$G - S$ is rendered as \texttt{(($\top$ : G.Subgraph).deleteVerts ↑S).coe}, so the component
count is \texttt{Nat.card} of \emph{that} graph's \texttt{ConnectedComponent}.  Using the \texttt{Subgraph}
API rather than \texttt{G.induce (↑S)$^{c}$} is what lets the "spanning subgraph" step be
stated at all, since $C - S$ and $G - S$ then live over the same vertex set.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.3: $\nu \ge 3$ and $\delta \ge \nu/2$ (stated as $\nu \le 2\delta$) imply $G$ is hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.dirac_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.dirac_hamiltonian}
If every vertex is joined to at least half the graph, there is enough adjacency
that a spanning cycle cannot be avoided.

$\delta \ge \nu/2$ is formalised as $\nu \le 2\delta$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid the
rounding ambiguity of $\nu/2$ under truncated division.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Lem 4.4.1: for nonadjacent $u,v$ with $d(u)+d(v) \ge \nu$, $G$ is hamiltonian iff $G+uv$ is]
\lean{SimpleGraph.bondy_chvatal}
\label{SimpleGraph.bondy_chvatal}
The book's proof is two sentences only because it \emph{reuses} the $S$/$T$ counting
argument (4.4) from Theorem 4.3.  In Lean that argument has to exist somewhere
concrete --- so this lemma, not Dirac, is the right place to write it out, and
Dirac then follows from the closure machinery.

Expanded, (4.4) is: from a Hamilton cycle of $G + uv$ that must use $uv$, extract
a Hamilton path $v_{1} \dots v_\nu$ in $G$ with $v_{1} = u$, $v_\nu = v$.  Put
$S = {v_{i} | u ~ v_{i+1}}$ and $T = {v_{i} | v_{i} ~ v}$.  Then $v_\nu \notin S \cup T$ gives
$|S \cup T| < \nu$, and $S \cap T = \emptyset$ because a common $v_{i}$ would close the Hamilton
cycle $v_{1} \dots v_{i} v_\nu v_{\nu-1} \dots v_{i+1} v_{1}$ in $G$.  Hence
$d(u) + d(v) = |S| + |T| < \nu$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.4 (honest restatement): reachability by closure steps preserves hamiltonicity]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_iff_of_closureSteps}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_iff_of_closureSteps}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
Stated in the file's "honest restatement" form: instead of positing a closure
operator, it says that if $H$ is reachable from $G$ by any finite chain of
\texttt{ClosureStep}s, then $G$ is hamiltonian exactly when $H$ is.  Taking $H$ to admit
no further step recovers the book's statement.

This restatement is what lets the file skip Lemma 4.4.2 entirely --- see below.

The book must prove $c(G)$ well defined before Theorem 4.4 can even be stated;
its proof (\S{}4.2, p. 64) is the argument:

Because this file quantifies over \texttt{ReflTransGen ClosureStep} chains rather than
naming a closure, \textbf{Lemma 4.4.2 is not needed and is not formalised}: the
statement above holds for \emph{every} chain, confluent or not.  It would only be
required if a \texttt{closure : SimpleGraph V $\to$ SimpleGraph V} function were introduced.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.4 (honest restatement): if closure steps reach $\top$, then $G$ was hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_of_closureSteps_top}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_of_closureSteps_top}
\uses{SimpleGraph.ClosureStep}
Stated with $\top$ in place of "$c(G)$ is complete", and \texttt{ClosureStep} reachability
in place of the closure operator.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Reusable helper (\textbf{!} absent from Mathlib): $\top$ on $\ge$ 3 vertices is hamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.top_isHamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.top_isHamiltonian}
In $K_{n}$ every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent, so any enumeration
$v_{1} v_{2} \dots v_n v_{1}$ is already a Hamilton cycle.  Three vertices are needed because
a cycle must have length at least three --- $K_{1}$ and $K_{2}$ have no cycle at all.

\textbf{!} Despite the book calling it "trivial", \textbf{Mathlib has no such lemma}, and it is
not trivial in Lean: it requires exhibiting a concrete cyclic enumeration of $V$
and proving the resulting walk is a cycle whose support is nodup and spans.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.5 (counting form): the Chv\'atal degree condition implies hamiltonicity]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian}
\textbf{!} The hypothesis is formalised in \textbf{counting form}, not by indexing the sorted
degree sequence.  The book's $d_m \le m$ says "at least $m$ vertices have degree
$\le m$", and $d_{\nu-m} < \nu - m$ says "at least $\nu - m$ vertices have degree
$< \nu - m$" --- precisely the two \texttt{Finset.filter} cardinalities in \texttt{hcond}.  This
avoids all $1$- versus $0$-indexing hazards around \texttt{degreeSequence}, at the cost
of no longer looking like the book's inequality.

The book's $m < \nu/2$ is written $2 * m < \nu$, and $m \ge 1$ is made explicit
(the book's $m$ is a degree $d'(u)$, and $m = 0$ is excluded by connectivity
considerations implicit in "as large as possible").
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Thm 4.6: a nonhamiltonian simple graph with $\nu \ge 3$ is degree-majorised by some $C_{m,\nu}$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_degree_majorised}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_degree_majorised}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Cmn, SimpleGraph.DegreeMajorised}
The family ${C_{m,\nu}}$ consists of the \textbf{degree-maximal} nonhamiltonian graphs:
any nonhamiltonian graph has degrees dominated, position by position, by one of
them.

Corollary 4.6 --- bounding the edge count of a nonhamiltonian graph reduces to
computing $\varepsilon(C_{m,\nu})$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.6a: $\varepsilon > C(\nu- 1,2) + 1$ implies hamiltonicity]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_edge_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_edge_bound}
Enough edges guarantee a spanning cycle, and this pins down exactly how many
"enough" is: a nonhamiltonian graph has at most $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$ edges.

"By theorem 1.1" is the handshaking lemma --- degree majorisation transfers to an
edge-count inequality because $2\varepsilon = \sum d(v)$.

\textbf{!} The book's algebra is over $\mathbb{Q}$ (note the $\tfrac{1}{2}$); in $\mathbb{N}$ the identity
$\tfrac{1}{2}(m^{2} + (\nu-2m)(\nu-m-1) + m(\nu-1)) = C(\nu-1,2) + 1 - \tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2) - (m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$
involves subtraction that truncates.  Either clear denominators and work with
$2\varepsilon$ throughout, or cast to $\mathbb{Z}$/$\mathbb{Q}$ for the identity and cast back.  The latter
is likely cleaner.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cor 4.6b: the extremal nonhamiltonian graphs at $C(\nu- 1,2)+1$ edges are $C_{1,\nu}$ (and $C_{2,5}$)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_extremal}
\label{SimpleGraph.ore_bondy_extremal}
\uses{SimpleGraph.Cmn}
The equality analysis of the first half.  The final inequality is tight only when
both subtracted terms $\tfrac{1}{2}(m-1)(m-2)$ and $(m-1)(\nu-2m-1)$ vanish, which happens
only for $m = 1$, or $m = 2$ together with $\nu = 5$.

So the bound is attained by exactly one graph for each $\nu$, plus one sporadic
extra at $\nu = 5$: the densest nonhamiltonian simple graphs there are.

\textbf{!} The book's closing "which is easily seen to imply that $G \cong C_{1,\nu}$" is
the hardest step to formalise, and it is \textbf{not} easy in Lean.  Degree sequence
does not in general determine a graph up to isomorphism; the implication holds
here only because of the specific structure of $C_{1,\nu}$ and $C_{2,5}$, and
recovering an explicit \texttt{$\simeq$g} requires constructing the vertex bijection by hand.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.1.4: no odd degree $\Rightarrow$ an edge-disjoint decomposition into cycles]
\lean{SimpleGraph.even_degree_cycle_decomposition}
\label{SimpleGraph.even_degree_cycle_decomposition}
Even degrees everywhere means no "loose ends".  Peel cycles off one at a time:
removing a cycle subtracts $2$ from the degree of each vertex it visits, so all
degrees stay even and the argument repeats until no edges are left.

"$E(G) = \bigcup E(C_{i})$ with the $C_{i}$ edge-disjoint" is rendered as the single
$\exists!$ statement --- every edge lies in exactly one of the cycles --- which packages
covering and disjointness together.

Note this needs \textbf{no connectivity hypothesis}: it is the local content of
Euler's theorem.  Connectivity is what additionally lets the cycles be spliced
into one tour (Theorem 4.1).
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.1.5: exactly $2k$ odd-degree vertices $\Rightarrow$ $k$ edge-disjoint covering trails]
\lean{SimpleGraph.odd_vertices_trail_cover}
\label{SimpleGraph.odd_vertices_trail_cover}
By Corollary 1.1 the odd-degree vertices come in pairs, so there are $k$ pairs.
Pair them up and add $k$ new edges joining the members of each pair; every vertex
of the enlarged graph then has even degree, so Theorem 4.1 gives an Euler tour.
Deleting the $k$ added edges cuts that tour into exactly $k$ trails, which are
edge-disjoint and between them cover every edge of $G$.

The practical reading: a road network with $2k$ awkward junctions needs $k$
separate pen-strokes; one Euler trail is the case $k = 1$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.1(a): not 2-connected (with $\nu \ge 3$) $\Rightarrow$ nonhamiltonian (restated on the repo\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_not_two_connected}
\label{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_not_two_connected}
\uses{SimpleGraph.vertexConnectivity}
A graph that is not 2-connected is either disconnected or has a cut vertex $v$.
Disconnected: no cycle reaches every vertex.  Cut vertex: take $S = {v}$ in
Theorem 4.2 --- deleting $v$ leaves at least two components, so
$\omega(G - S) \ge 2 > 1 = |S|$, violating the necessary condition.

A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex and returns, which needs two independent
routes out of every vertex --- exactly 2-connectivity.  Necessary but far from
sufficient (the Petersen graph is 3-connected and nonhamiltonian).

Stated against this file's local \texttt{vertexConnectivity}, not the one in
\texttt{Connectivity.lean} --- see the warning on that definition above.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.1(b): an unbalanced bipartite graph is nonhamiltonian]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_unbalanced_bipartite}
\label{SimpleGraph.nonhamiltonian_of_unbalanced_bipartite}
Every edge crosses between $X$ and $Y$, so a cycle alternates sides and uses
equally many vertices from each.  A Hamilton cycle uses \emph{all} vertices, forcing
$|X| = |Y|$.

This is why the book's Herschel graph is nonhamiltonian:

(\S{}4.2, p. 61.)  Equivalently, apply Theorem 4.2 with $S$ the smaller side.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.3: a Hamilton path implies $\omega(G - S) \le |S| + 1$]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_toughness}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_toughness}
The path analogue of Theorem 4.2.  Deleting $k$ vertices from a \emph{path} breaks it
into at most $k + 1$ pieces --- one more than for a cycle, because a path has two
loose ends rather than being closed up.  The Hamilton path $P$ is a spanning
subgraph of $G$, so $\omega(G - S) \le \omega(P - S) \le |S| + 1$.

The extra $+1$ is the price of not closing the cycle, making the condition
weaker --- as it must be, since a Hamilton path is weaker than a Hamilton cycle.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.4*: Chv\'atal's Hamilton-path degree condition (counting form)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian_path}
\label{SimpleGraph.chvatal_hamiltonian_path}
The Hamilton-\emph{path} counterpart of Theorem 4.5, with thresholds shifted by one.
Formalised in counting form, exactly as Theorem 4.5 is --- see the note there on
why indexing the sorted sequence is avoided.

Note the strict $d_m < m$ here versus $d_m \le m$ in Theorem 4.5; the \texttt{hcond}
filters use $<$ accordingly.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.5: a self-complementary graph has a Hamilton path (Clapham)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_of_self_complementary}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_of_self_complementary}
Only part (b) is formalised --- part (a) has no separate declaration in this file.

Part (b) from part (a): if $G \cong G^{c}$ the two sorted degree sequences are
\emph{identical}, so $d_m \ge d_m'$ holds trivially at every index.

Recall from exercise 1.2.11(b) that self-complementary graphs exist only when
$\nu \equiv 0$ or \texttt{1 (mod 4)}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.5(a) (Clapham): if $G$ dominates $G^{c}$ on the lower half of the sorted degree sequence, $G$ has a\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_of_degree_dominates_compl}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonian_path_of_degree_dominates_compl}
This file previously formalised only part (b)
(\texttt{hamiltonian\_path\_of\_self\_complementary}), even though the book deduces (b) \emph{from}
(a) --- so (a) was a hidden prerequisite with no declaration.  The triage
(\texttt{log/graphtheory-EXERCISE\_TRIAGE.md} \S{}A.3) recorded this as a fidelity gap and
recommended stating (a).  Nothing here is invented: the statement is the book's
own, quoted above.

The two sorted degree sequences are rendered the way \texttt{chvatal\_hamiltonian\_path}
renders its sequence --- via a sorting equiv $\sigma$ on \texttt{Fin $\nu$} making the degrees
\texttt{Antitone}/\texttt{Monotone} --- rather than as raw lists, so the two conditions in this file
are stated in the same idiom and can share lemmas.

$m \le \nu/2$ is written $2 * m \le \nu$ to avoid $\mathbb{N}$-division.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.8: Erd\H{o}s' edge bound $\nu \ge 6\delta$, $\varepsilon > C(\nu-\delta,2) + \delta^{2}$\dots]
\lean{SimpleGraph.erdos_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.erdos_hamiltonian}
Corollary 4.6 gives a sufficient edge count taking no account of the minimum
degree.  Erd\H{o}s' refinement: when $\delta$ is known and small relative to $\nu$, a weaker
count suffices --- $C(\nu-\delta, 2) + \delta^{2}$ rather than $C(\nu-1, 2) + 1$.

The shape of the bound reflects the extremal configuration: a clique on $\nu - \delta$
vertices with $\delta$ low-degree vertices attached, the densest way to be
nonhamiltonian while holding the minimum degree at $\delta$.  $\nu \ge 6\delta$ keeps $\delta$
genuinely small.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.9*: connected with $\nu > 2\delta$ $\Rightarrow$ a path of length $\ge$ $2\delta$ (Dirac)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.long_path_of_order_gt_two_minDegree}
\label{SimpleGraph.long_path_of_order_gt_two_minDegree}
Exercise 1.6.3 already gives a path of length $\delta$ from the minimum degree alone;
Dirac's sharpening doubles that, at the cost of connectivity and $\nu > 2\delta$.

The bracketed cycle version --- 2-connected, $\nu \ge 2\delta$, cycle of length $\ge 2\delta$ --- is
\textbf{stated but not proved} in the chapter.  It is what exercise 4.2.10 relies on;
see the warning there.  It is not stated in this file either.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.10: a $2k$-regular graph on $4k+1$ vertices is hamiltonian (Nash-Williams)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.nash_williams_regular_hamiltonian}
\label{SimpleGraph.nash_williams_regular_hamiltonian}
Such a graph has $\delta = \Delta = 2k$ and $\nu = 4k + 1 = 2\delta + 1$, one vertex above the
threshold $\nu \ge 2\delta$ of Dirac's cycle remark.  That remark yields a cycle of length
at least $2\delta = 4k$ --- missing at most one vertex --- and regularity plus parity then
force the cycle to pick up the last vertex too.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $k \ge 1$.  At $k = 0$ the statement reads
"every $0$-regular graph on $1$ vertex is hamiltonian", which is false in
Mathlib: a Hamilton cycle needs length $\ge 3$, so the one-vertex graph is not
\texttt{IsHamiltonian}.  The hypothesis $1 \le k$ must be added.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Ex 4.2.11(a): a Hamilton-connected graph satisfies $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ (Moon)]
\lean{SimpleGraph.hamiltonConnected_edge_bound}
\label{SimpleGraph.hamiltonConnected_edge_bound}
\uses{SimpleGraph.IsHamiltonConnected}
Hamilton-connectedness demands a spanning path between \emph{every} pair, forcing many
edges.  Every vertex must have degree at least $3$: a degree-$2$ vertex has both
its edges forced into any spanning path through it as an interior vertex, leaving
no way to make it an endpoint of a spanning path to a third vertex.  Summing
$d(v) \ge 3$ and applying handshaking gives $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu$, and a parity refinement
pushes this to $2\varepsilon \ge 3\nu + 1$.

Formalised as $3\nu + 1 \le 2\varepsilon$ to stay in the natural numbers and avoid the ceiling.

\textbf{!} The Lean signature omits the book's $\nu \ge 4$.  It is needed: for $\nu = 3$,
$\top$ on three vertices is Hamilton-connected with $\varepsilon = 3$, but $3\nu + 1 = 10 > 6 = 2\varepsilon$.
So the statement as written is \textbf{false at $\nu = 3$} and \texttt{4 $\le$ Fintype.card V} must
be added.
\end{theorem}
